First, our original mapping was not valid non-perturbatively in , since it did not include non-local correlations between the gravity fields which appear at finite . The theory in the bulk contains additional auxiliary fields which implement the finite constraints. Second, we discuss the generalization of our mapping to the field theory on , and in particular how the sphere free energy matches exactly between the two sides, and how the mapping can be consistently regularized. Finally, we discuss the field theory at finite temperature, and show that the low-temperature phase of the vector models can be mapped to a high-spin gravity theory on thermal AdS space.

children.title: Abstract
children.body: In previous work we constructed an explicit mapping between large vector models (free or critical) in dimensions and a non-local high-spin gravity theory on , such that the gravitational theory reproduces the field theory correlation functions order by order in . In this paper we discuss three aspects of this mapping. First, our original mapping was not valid non-perturbatively in , since it did not include non-local correlations between the gravity fields which appear at finite . We show that by using a bi-local type formalism similar to the one used in the SYK model, we can construct an exact mapping to the bulk that is valid also at finite . The theory in the bulk contains additional auxiliary fields which implement the finite constraints. Second, we discuss the generalization of our mapping to the field theory on , and in particular how the sphere free energy matches exactly between the two sides, and how the mapping can be consistently regularized. Finally, we discuss the field theory at finite temperature, and show that the low-temperature phase of the vector models can be mapped to a high-spin gravity theory on thermal AdS space.

One of the simplest examples of the AdS/CFT correspondence [1] is the duality between the -singlet sector of the theory of free complex scalar fields in space-time dimensions () and a high-spin gravity theory on [2]. This example is free on the field theory side, and weakly coupled on the gravity side at large , so in the large limit both sides are controllable (and this remains true also after deforming to the critical vector model). This suggests that at least order by order in it should be possible to explicitly map the field theory to the gravity side. Such an explicit mapping was presented in [3] (following [4]1); it rewrites the field theory as a non-local bulk theory of massless spin fields on , whose coupling constant is . This mapping is derived by first changing variables in the field theory from the fields () to a -invariant bi-local field

(1.1)

Then, the bi-local field is expanded in irreducible representations of the conformal group (we work in Euclidean space for simplicity). It was shown in [3] that the expansion of massless transverse traceless spin fields on (with ) in representations of contains precisely the same representations, allowing a linear mapping (consistent with conformal invariance) between and the bulk fields. It was conjectured that the resulting bulk action is equivalent in the classical limit to Vasiliev’s high-spin gravity theory on [7, 8, 9] (believed to be the unique consistent classical theory of high-spin fields on ), gauge-fixed such that it lives on a fixed background and such that the spin fields are transverse and traceless2. Assuming that this is true, one may view the construction of [3] as providing an action for this high-spin gravity theory, which enables for the first time both the computation of the action for classical solutions, and a systematic evaluation of quantum corrections.

gist.html: An earlier paper rewrote free vector models as a non-local high-spin bulk theory, via a bilocal expanded in conformal representations.

children.title: Vector models and the high-spin duality
children.body: In a vector model the singlet operators of lowest dimension are bilinears $\sum_I\phi_I^*\partial^J\phi_I$, one for each spin $J$. In the free model those with $J\ge1$ are conserved currents, so the theory has an infinite tower of conserved high-spin currents. In AdS/CFT a conserved spin-$J$ current is dual to a massless spin-$J$ gauge field, so the gravity dual of the free model's singlet sector must be a high-spin gravity, with a massless field of every spin and the graviton at $J=2$. Klebanov and Polyakov proposed this duality in 2002 for the critical $O(N)$ model and Vasiliev's theory in $AdS_4$, the free model differing only by the boundary condition of the bulk scalar. Singlet correlators factorize at large $N$, so the bulk is weakly coupled, with $G_N\sim1/N$. Unlike most holographic dualities, both sides are then tractable, which is why an explicit map from one to the other seems within reach.

The existence of an explicit off-shell mapping between field theory and bulk gravity path integrals, as constructed in [3], is highly non-trivial. The construction guarantees that any bulk computations of correlation functions on will match with the free field theory perturbatively in , but many aspects of the mapping are not yet clear. In this paper we discuss three aspects and generalizations of the mapping of [3].

gist.html: That off-shell map matches correlators perturbatively in $1/N$, but many of its aspects remain unclear.

children.body: In Section 2 we discuss how to perform the mapping for finite values of . The mapping of [3] was constructed such that it is valid order by order in the expansion. However, for finite the bi-local fields (1.1) obey constraints on products of such fields that were not taken into account in [3], and which translate into similar constraints on products of bulk fields that must arise at finite . We can take this into account by introducing3 independent bi-local fields and , such that is a Lagrange multiplier implementing the condition that is equal to (1.1). This is similar to the standard method used, for instance, in the SYK model [15] (for vector models this was previously done for instance in [16], and the new thing we are doing is mapping this to the bulk). Integrating over the fields leads to an action for and which properly takes the constraints into account even at finite . We can then map this action to the bulk, obtaining an extra set of bulk fields which come from the auxiliary field . The fields may be viewed as auxiliary fields in the bulk, which implement also there the appropriate finite constraints; performing the path integral over them order by order in reproduces the bulk action of [3], but keeping them gives a consistent bulk theory even at finite . Note that even at finite we can map the CFT to fields living on a fixed AdS background, and we do not need to introduce any sum over different geometries or topologies; presumably this is a special feature of high-spin gravity theories.

gist.html: A Lagrange-multiplier bilocal $\Sigma$ makes the map exact at finite $N$; its bulk image, auxiliary fields, imposes the constraints.

children.title: The G–Σ formalism in the SYK model
children.body: The Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (SYK) model has $N$ Majorana fermions $\chi_i(t)$ with random couplings among $q$ of them at a time. After averaging over the couplings, the action depends on the fermions only through the bilocal $G(t_1,t_2)=\frac1N\sum_i\chi_i(t_1)\chi_i(t_2)$. One inserts a delta function setting $G$ equal to this bilinear, written as an integral over a Lagrange multiplier $\Sigma(t_1,t_2)$, and integrates out the fermions, which now appear only quadratically. The result is an exact action, $N$ times a functional of $G$ and $\Sigma$ containing $\log\operatorname{Pf}(\partial_t-\Sigma)$. At large $N$ its saddle-point equations are the Schwinger–Dyson equations, but nothing in the rewriting assumed large $N$. This $G$–$\Sigma$ formalism is what the paper applies to the vector model, where $\Sigma$ has usually been integrated out; keeping it retains the finite-$N$ information.

In Section 3 we discuss the generalization of the mapping of [3], which was written for the field theory on , to a finite volume space, focusing on the sphere . The generalization to is straightforward, since the theory on is related to the theory on by a conformal transformation. However, understanding this generalization enables us to discuss two issues explicitly. First, the free energy on is finite (for finite ) and is one of the simplest observables in the vector models, so it is interesting to see how it is reproduced by the bulk gravitational theory. We find that in our finite formalism the sphere free energy is reproduced in a trivial way; it comes from a pre-factor in front of the bulk path integral, and does not receive any classical or quantum contributions from the bulk path integral. In the past, quantum corrections to naive versions of the bulk path integral of high-spin gravity (with specific off-shell continuations of Vasiliev’s equations of motion) were compared to the field theory result [17], suggesting that for theories the gravitational bulk coupling is actually . We argue that in our case4 the bulk computation is actually different than what was assumed in previous works, and it does not suggest any such shift. Second, explicit computations, both in the bi-local formalism and in the bulk, require regularization. We discuss for the theory on which regularizations are needed on both sides, and how we can perform the mapping between the two sides for the regulated theories in a way that ensures that a consistent mapping will arise when the regulators are taken to infinity. Additional details of this are described in an appendix.

gist.html: On $S^d$ the sphere free energy is a prefactor of the bulk path integral, and the regulators of both sides can be matched.

children.body: Finally, in Section 4 we discuss the mapping to the bulk at finite temperature. Imposing the projection to singlets at finite temperature is more complicated and requires introducing and integrating over a holonomy, and we do not know how to map the field theory with the holonomy to the bulk. However, at large , the integral over the holonomy is governed by a saddle point. In particular if we take the large limit before the large volume limit, the theory is in a low-temperature “confining” phase governed by a uniform distribution of the holonomy eigenvalues, while if we take the large volume limit first, the theory is in a “deconfined” phase with the holonomy matrix equal to the identity matrix. In the former case we show that at leading order in the saddle point approximation we can use the same mapping to the bulk as for zero temperature, and we obtain the same bulk theory but on a thermal AdS space, as expected. In the latter case we argue that the mapping must be modified, and presumably this corresponds to a bulk theory on some “black hole” background; we leave the understanding of this case to future work.

gist.html: In the confined phase the thermal theory maps to high-spin gravity on thermal AdS; the deconfined phase is left open.
The explicit vector-model map extends to finite $N$ with auxiliary bulk fields, to the sphere, and to thermal AdS.

brief.html: An earlier paper rewrote the singlet sector of $N$ free scalars as a non-local high-spin gravity on $AdS_{d+1}$, by expanding the bilocal $G(x_1,x_2)$ in conformal representations; it holds order by order in $1/N$. A Lagrange-multiplier bilocal $\Sigma$ makes it exact at finite $N$, with auxiliary bulk fields imposing the constraints and no sum over geometries. On $S^d$ the free energy comes from a prefactor, and the regulators can be matched. The low-temperature phase maps to thermal AdS; the high-temperature phase is left open.

children.body: In this section we derive the AdS dual of a theory of free scalar fields at finite . We start by reviewing how [18] mapped the path integral of free complex scalar fields5 to a path integral of -invariant bilocals , which is only valid at large since at finite the bilocals obey constraints that were ignored. We then show how to make the bilocal path integral valid at finite by introducing a new bilocal field , and demonstrate how this path integral exhibits the expected finite constraints. We then describe how to map the finite bilocal theory to the bulk, as was done at large in [3], and show how the finite constraints set the amplitude of empty AdS to zero. Finally, we generalize to the critical theory.

children.title: Collective fields and why the bilocal is classical
children.body: The collective field method of Jevicki and Sakita rewrites a theory of $N$ fields in terms of invariant composites, here the bilocal $G(x_1,x_2)$. The change of variables has a Jacobian, a power of $\det G$, and the action becomes a function of $G$ alone. Both are proportional to $N$ at large $N$, so $N$ multiplies the whole bilocal action and $1/N$ plays the role of $\hbar$. The bilocal is then classical at large $N$: its saddle point is the exact large-$N$ two-point function, here the free propagator $G_0$, and fluctuations around it are suppressed by powers of $1/N$. For free fields the $1/N$ expansion of singlet correlators is exact and simple, so the many interactions of the collective field must cancel order by order. A collective field is not an independent field, though: it inherits constraints from its definition, which a large-$N$ expansion never sees.

gist.html: The older bilocal path integral carries $|\det G|^{N-V}$, so its continuum limit needs large $N$ first.

brief.html: The free theory of $N$ complex scalars, regulated on a lattice of $V$ points, is rewritten in terms of the bilocal $G$. A delta function, written with a multiplier $\tilde\Sigma$, fixes $G$, and the scalars are integrated out. Integrating out $\tilde\Sigma$ leaves a weight $|\det G|^{N-V}$ that converges only for $V\le N$, so the continuum needs large $N$ first. Its large-$N$ saddle is the free propagator, and the free answers emerge only through cancellations at every order in $1/N$.

children.title: Harmonic analysis on the conformal group
children.body: Functions of two points that transform like a product of two operators of dimension $\Delta_0$ can be expanded in conformal partial waves, much as functions on a line are expanded in plane waves. This is harmonic analysis on the Euclidean conformal group $SO(d+1,1)$, worked out by Dobrev, Mack, Petkova, Petrova and Todorov. Each partial wave is a three-point structure $\langle\mathcal O_{\Delta_0}\mathcal O_{\Delta_0}\mathcal O_{\Delta,J}\rangle$, labelled by a spin $J$ and a dimension $\Delta=d/2+is$ on the principal series, and together they form a complete orthogonal basis. The dimension $d-\Delta$, the shadow, labels the same representation. In AdS the same labels classify solutions of the wave equation: a spin-$J$ field of mass $M^2=\Delta(\Delta-d)-J$ has bulk-to-boundary propagators of dimension $\Delta$. Expanding both sides over one group and matching them representation by representation is the core of the map.

children.body: A bulk scalar of mass $m^2$ in $AdS_{d+1}$ behaves near the boundary as $z^{\Delta_-}$ or $z^{\Delta_+}$, with $\Delta_\pm=\frac d2\pm\sqrt{\frac{d^2}4+m^2}$. When both falloffs are allowed there are two consistent boundary conditions, dual to an operator of dimension $\Delta_-$ or $\Delta_+=d-\Delta_-$. Deforming the CFT by a double-trace term $f\,\mathcal O^2$, with $\mathcal O$ of dimension $\Delta_-$, starts a renormalization group flow whose infrared end has $\mathcal O$ of dimension $\Delta_+$; in the bulk the flow only changes the boundary condition, as Witten and Gubser and Klebanov showed. In the free vector model $\sum_I|\phi_I|^2$ has dimension $d-2$, and the quartic interaction is exactly such a double-trace deformation; at the critical point the scalar has dimension 2. The paper finds the same mechanism off-shell, as a constraint on the boundary falloff of $\Phi_0$.

We start by discussing how the AdS/CFT map discussed in the previous section for flat infinite space generalizes to the sphere . We then use our finite formalism to schematically map the sphere free energy from the CFT to the bulk, and compare to previous computations in the literature. To make this map completely rigorous, we need to provide consistent regularizations in both the CFT and the bulk, which we discuss in the last subsection.

In the previous section, we discussed the AdS/CFT map that takes a field theory defined on to a bulk theory defined on AdS with metric (2.23), which corresponds to the upper half space with a conformal boundary . We will now take the field theory to live on , and map it to the dimensional hyperbolic space with metric

The AdS/CFT maps in Section 2.3 can thus be adapted to the sphere by simply replacing all instances of the metric, such as occur for integration measures (in the CFT or on the boundary of AdS) and lengths, by the metric, and replacing the 3-point functions and bulk-to-boundary propagators appearing in the equations by the same objects on .

children.title: The sphere free energy of a CFT
children.body: For a CFT on the round sphere $S^d$, the free energy $F=-\log Z$ is a natural observable: the sphere has no scale besides its radius, and $F$ depends on it only through ultraviolet divergences. In odd $d$ the finite part is universal, and in $d=3$ the $F$-theorem says that it decreases along renormalization group flows, so it counts degrees of freedom. A free complex scalar gives about $0.13$ in $d=3$, and $N$ of them give $N$ times that. In holography the leading term, of order $N$ here, is the classical bulk action, and the corrections of order one come from one-loop determinants of all bulk fields. In high-spin gravity this one-loop sum runs over infinitely many spins and needs a regularization, usually with zeta functions. The paper finds instead that in its finite-$N$ formalism no bulk term contributes to the sphere free energy at all.

Note that in (3.3) we chose a specific normalization of the sphere free energy, which is the same as the one of free fields and is not affected by imposing the singlet condition. In general imposing the singlet condition could modify the free energy by multiplying it by a constant (for instance this happens if in it is imposed by coupling to a Chern-Simons gauge field at infinite level). In any computation of the sphere free energy one needs to specify the normalization chosen, and we discuss here how our particular normalization follows from the bulk actions we derived.

gist.html: That normalization is the one of $N$ free fields; other ways of imposing the singlet condition could change it.

If we want to write this constant term directly in a bulk language then we need to find a corresponding regularization in the bulk, and we will discuss this in the next subsection.

children.body: It is interesting to contrast our calculation of the sphere free energy with previous computations in the literature. In our derivation, the non-zero contribution to the free energy sits outside the path integral, which is why our calculation is immediate. Previous attempts to compute the free energy, starting with [17] with many followups [23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31], were hampered by the lack of an explicit action for the high-spin gravity theory in the bulk. In the absence of an action, the leading large free energy could not be computed. However, the 1-loop correction can still be derived if one assumes that the (off-shell) kinetic term in the bulk action takes the canonical two-derivative form for each spin, in which case the 1-loop correction can be computed by summing over the contributions of all physical and ghost modes that arise from a certain gauge fixing of this conjectured quadratic action. In the case of complex free scalars with global symmetry, the resulting 1-loop correction was found to vanish as expected, while in the case of real free scalars with global symmetry , the 1-loop correction was found to be identical to the tree level term. This was justified by assuming that the dictionary should be modified to in this case. However, when the calculation was generalized to other examples of higher spin AdS/CFT in [23], such as the duality of fermionic vector models in odd , it was found that no such shift could explain the nonvanishing 1-loop free energy.

gist.html: Earlier one-loop tests assumed two-derivative kinetic terms; they matched for $U(N)$ but needed a shifted coupling for $O(N)$.

children.body: We now see that these previous calculations were unjustified in assuming that the off-shell quadratic action takes the canonical two-derivative term, as we see explicitly from our bulk action which has quartic-in-derivatives kinetic terms; the form of the off-shell action does not follow from just from the field content in the bulk. We thus see the “match” of the 1-loop correction for the case as a coincidence, and the mismatch in all other cases as unsurprising.

gist.html: The bulk action's kinetic terms are quartic in derivatives, so that assumption fails and the $U(N)$ match is a coincidence.

children.body: In the case of the critical vector models discussed in Section 2.5, the sphere free energy will receive corrections order by order in , which by construction will agree between the field theory and the gravity computations.

gist.html: For the critical models the $1/N$ corrections to the sphere free energy agree by construction.
Both sides give $Z_\phi^N$ from a prefactor; earlier one-loop tests assumed a kinetic term the bulk action does not have.

brief.html: In the finite-$N$ formalism, integrating out $\eta$ sets $\Sigma$ to zero, so $Z=Z_\phi^N$, the normalization of $N$ free fields, with no vacuum diagrams at all. With unit Jacobian the bulk gives exactly the same prefactor, with no loop contributions. In the large-$N$ formalism loops would have to cancel against the Jacobian. Earlier one-loop tests assumed two-derivative kinetic terms. This bulk action is quartic in derivatives, so their $U(N)$ match looks coincidental, and no shift of the coupling is suggested for $O(N)$.

children.body: We now discuss how to consistently regularize the theories on either side of the duality. Note that in the finite theory of Section 2.2 there are no loop diagrams, so a regularization is only needed for the vacuum amplitude discussed above; however, in the formalism of Section 2.1 any computation must be regularized to make sense.

gist.html: The finite-$N$ theory needs regularization only for the vacuum amplitude; the large-$N$ formalism needs it everywhere.

children.body: Our AdS/CFT mapping has been defined formally on the unregulated theories on either side of the duality, but to ensure that it really works, one must become convinced that the theories can somehow be consistently regularized. This means that a mapping must be found between regulated, finite “versions” of either theory, which approaches the continuum mapping as the regulator is removed.

gist.html: A rigorous map must connect regulated, finite versions of both theories and approach the continuum map.

children.body: On the field theory side, the CFT on the sphere is automatically IR regulated, and needs only to be UV regulated. One possible regulator which we discussed above is a lattice, but this breaks all the symmetries, so its analysis is very complicated. An alternative regulator is a hard cutoff on the eigenvalues of the Laplacian operator (acting on the original scalar fields) (with ), which is sufficient to make the theory finite in the sense that the space of allowed bi-local fields is a finite-dimensional linear subspace of the unregulated one. Such a regulator breaks the conformal symmetry down to the sphere’s isometries , and we analyze how many modes remain in each representation in appendix A.1.

gist.html: In the CFT a cutoff on the Laplacian's eigenvalues keeps $SO(d+1)$ and leaves finitely many bilocal modes.

children.body: In the bulk hyperbolic space (3.1) on the other hand, in order to get a finite number of modes one needs a UV regulator (say, a cutoff on the bulk Laplacian operator ) as well as an IR regulator (say, boundary conditions at some finite radius ), because the Laplacian has a continuous spectrum in hyperbolic space. These cutoffs can be chosen to be equal for every field of spin or to depend on the spin. The IR regulator breaks the bulk isometries , mirroring the conformal field theory. Again the regulators restrict the space of fields to a finite subspace.

gist.html: The bulk needs both UV and IR cutoffs; the IR one breaks its isometries to $SO(d+1)$, as in the CFT.

children.body: It is not easy to directly map the CFT regulator to the bulk or vice versa, since each regulator becomes very complicated when expressed in the other language. However, in order to construct a finite invertible mapping between the regulated theories on both sides, we do not necessarily need to have precisely the same regulator; it is enough that we have the same number of surviving modes in each representation. This is because the map organizes itself into “diagonal blocks” corresponding to the surviving irreducible representations, and if each block is a square, a generic map like ours will be invertible with probability 1. Namely, we can either use the CFT-to-AdS mapping on the first line of (2.28) on the modes that survive in the CFT, and its inverse to give us a regulated AdS-to-CFT mapping, or we can use the AdS-to-CFT mapping on the second line of (2.28) on the modes that survive in the bulk, and its inverse will give us a regulated CFT-to-AdS mapping; the two options are different but both will reproduce the theory we want in the limit where the regulators are removed.

gist.html: The regulators need not correspond, only the mode counts per $SO(d+1)$ representation; the blockwise map is then generically invertible.

children.body: It can be argued (see appendix A) that by taking the IR and UV regulators in the bulk to vary in some specific relation to the UV regulator of the CFT , the degeneracy of each representation on the bulk side can be made to agree with the degeneracy in the CFT side. The precise choice of regulators may be complicated, but it can be computed if necessary. Making this choice leads to a precise mapping between the regulated theories on both sides (though not one that is conducive to explicit computations).

gist.html: Bulk cutoffs tuned to the CFT cutoff can be argued to match every degeneracy: a precise, if impractical, regulated map.

children.body: It should also be stated that there are some subtleties to IR regularization in the bulk – specifically the choice of boundary conditions in the bulk – due to the presence of high-spin fields in a prescribed gauge. The simplest boundary condition that makes sense is a Dirichlet condition on the completely parallel (to the boundary) and traceless (with respect to the boundary metric) components of the tensors, and it is sufficient to make the theory finite. However with this choice, somewhat inconveniently, the Laplacian is not self-adjoint (and the eigentensors correspondingly are not orthogonal) with respect to the standard inner product. It appears that no choice of boundary condition makes the Laplacian both self-adjoint and complete, but completeness appears to be sufficient to make the theory well-defined. The situation can be improved somewhat by changing the inner product into one with respect to which the Laplacian is both self-adjoint and complete, but this sacrifices “locality” in some sense, since the path integral cannot be interpreted as summing over sections of some vector bundle. Since the bulk action is not quite local to begin with, this isn’t too much of a problem, and locality is restored as the cutoff is removed (the modified inner product approaches the standard one of hyperbolic space).

gist.html: No bulk boundary condition seems to make the Laplacian both self-adjoint and complete; completeness appears to suffice.

children.body: It’s instructive to compare the theory under consideration with perturbative general relativity, which is a theory of a symmetric (but not, in general, traceless) rank-2 tensor. As discussed in [32], the choice of boundary conditions here is nontrivial, and ultimately involves, in one way or another, the conformal mode (the trace part) of the rank-2 tensor, which is absent in the higher-spin theory. We speculate however, that some fluctuations in the theory should perhaps be identified as “trace-parts” of others - they have the right scaling dimensions (in the sense of the CFT) and a “wrong-sign” kinetic term, much like the conformal mode in linearized general relativity. It is conceivable that boundary conditions that mix the high-spin fields with their trace-parts in some elaborate way could give a more well-behaved IR-regulated theory, but this investigation is left for future work.

gist.html: Some fluctuations may play the part of general relativity's conformal mode, with wrong-sign kinetic terms; left for future work.
Regulated theories can be matched by keeping equally many modes in each $SO(d+1)$ representation on both sides.

brief.html: A rigorous map must connect finite, regulated versions of both theories, and approach the continuum map as the regulators are removed. The CFT on $S^d$ needs only a UV cutoff on the Laplacian, which keeps $SO(d+1)$; hyperbolic space needs UV and IR cutoffs, which break its isometries to the same $SO(d+1)$. The regulators need not correspond: if each $SO(d+1)$ representation keeps equally many modes, the map splits into square blocks that are generically invertible. Bulk cutoffs tied to the CFT's can be argued to achieve this.

gist.html: On $S^d$ the map carries over; the sphere free energy is a prefactor, and the regulators of both sides can be matched.

brief.html: Because $S^d$ is conformal to $\mathbb{R}^d$, the map carries over to hyperbolic space, with $L_2$ normalizability as the bulk boundary condition. In the finite-$N$ formalism the sphere partition function is $Z_\phi^N$ on both sides, a prefactor with no classical or loop contribution. Earlier one-loop comparisons assumed two-derivative kinetic terms, which this bulk action does not have. A rigorous version needs regulated theories on both sides; matching their mode counts in each $SO(d+1)$ representation is argued to be enough.

In a general dimension it is not clear how to introduce this holonomy in a local way without introducing additional degrees of freedom or flux sectors; for this can be done [33] by coupling the vector models to a Chern-Simons theory and taking .

children.title: Singlet projection and the holonomy
children.body: To keep only $U(N)$ singlets in a thermal trace, one averages the action of the group over $U(N)$, which is the singlet projection. In the Euclidean path integral this is a gauge field $A_t$ on the thermal circle, constant in space, whose only gauge-invariant content is the holonomy $U=e^{i\int_0^\beta A_t\,dt}$; the scalars become periodic up to this twist. Integrating over the eigenvalues $e^{i\theta_k}$ of the holonomy gives a matrix integral which, at large $N$, is dominated by one distribution of the $\theta_k$ on the circle. If it is uniform, every $\operatorname{Tr}U^n$ with $n\ne0$ vanishes and only singlets are counted: the confined phase. If it is localized near $\theta=0$, the traces are of order $N$ and the system behaves almost like $N$ free fields: the deconfined phase. These traces, Polyakov loops, are the order parameters.

On general grounds, we expect in the large limit (with volume ) a phase transition between a low-temperature “confined phase” where low-dimension -singlets dominate the path integral, and a high-temperature “deconfined phase” whose thermodynamics can be approximated by ignoring the -singlet constraint. Schematically, we can think of the “confined” singlet degrees of freedom as the bi-local fields whose number scales as such that their free energy scales as , while the number of “deconfined” degrees of freedom scales as , so their free energy scales as . This suggests that the large phase transition should occur when , and indeed this is what was found for the case on in [34]. Both phases may be described by large saddle points in the integral over the holonomy. In the confined phase in the large limit the eigenvalue distribution of the saddle-point holonomy for is approximately uniform, while in the deconfined phase the distribution is localized and all the eigenvalues approach one as .

gist.html: A transition at $T^{d-1}V\simeq N$ separates uniform holonomy eigenvalues (confined) from eigenvalues near one (deconfined).

children.title: Thermal AdS and the Hawking–Page transition
children.body: A CFT at temperature $T$ on a sphere is dual to gravity in a spacetime whose boundary is $S^{d-1}\times S^1_\beta$. Two smooth Euclidean geometries fill it in: thermal AdS, global AdS with periodic Euclidean time, and the Euclidean AdS black hole, in which the thermal circle shrinks to zero at the horizon. Thermal AdS has a free energy of order one, the black hole one of order $1/G_N$. Hawking and Page found that the black hole dominates above a temperature of order the inverse AdS radius, and Witten identified this Hawking–Page transition with deconfinement in large-$N$ gauge theories: the Polyakov loop vanishes in thermal AdS but not in the black hole. In vector models the transition sits instead at $T^{d-1}V\sim N$, and the paper maps only the thermal AdS side.

For simplicity we discuss here the theory in infinite flat space. The discussion above makes it clear that the results in the large limit will depend on the order of limits between taking large and taking large ; if we take large first we will always be in the confined low-temperature phase, while if we take large first we will always be in the deconfined high-temperature phase. Presumably, we need a different ‘black hole’ geometry (as suggested also by the fact that the traces of the holonomy matrix are non-vanishing) and a different mapping in order to incorporate these periodicities in the bulk, and it would be interesting to understand how to do this.

gist.html: In the deconfined phase the bilocal is periodic in each time separately; presumably a black-hole map is needed, left open.
In the confined phase the bilocal's effective period is $N\beta$, and the zero-temperature map yields high-spin gravity on thermal AdS.

brief.html: At finite temperature the singlet projection requires integrating over a $U(N)$ holonomy; at large $N$ its eigenvalues are uniform in the confined phase and near one in the deconfined phase. gist.html:
• Context An earlier explicit map turns vector models into non-local high-spin gravity on $AdS_{d+1}$, order by order in $1/N$.
  • Result
    • A bilocal Lagrange multiplier, as in SYK, makes the map exact at finite $N$; its bulk image, auxiliary fields on one fixed AdS, imposes the finite-$N$ constraints.
    • On the sphere the free energy matches exactly, as a prefactor of the bulk path integral; matching mode counts can regularize the map consistently.
    • The low-temperature phase maps to high-spin gravity on thermal AdS.
  • Why it matters Assuming the conjectured equivalence with Vasiliev's theory, such a map gives high-spin gravity an action whose quantum corrections can be computed systematically.

brief.html:
An earlier paper by the authors turned the $U(N)$-singlet sector of $N$ free complex scalars in $d>2$ dimensions into a bulk theory on $AdS_{d+1}$. It expands the bilocal $G(x_1,x_2)=\frac1N\sum_I\phi_I^*(x_1)\phi_I(x_2)$ in conformal representations and matches them to massless spin-$J$ fields $\Phi_J$. The result is a non-local high-spin gravity with coupling $1/N$, conjectured to be a gauge-fixed form of Vasiliev's theory, which reproduces the field theory order by order in $1/N$. The paper studies three aspects of this map: finite $N$, the sphere $S^d$, and finite temperature.

First, at finite $N$ the bilocal obeys constraints: on a lattice of $V$ points it is a matrix of rank at most $N$. The earlier bilocal path integral ignores these; its weight $|\det G|^{N-V}$ even diverges unless $N\ge V$, so the continuum limit needs large $N$ first. The fix, borrowed from the SYK model, keeps the Lagrange multiplier $\Sigma$ that defines $G$ as an independent bilocal field. Because $\Sigma$ never contracts with itself, the resulting theory has no loop diagrams: each correlator is one tree diagram equal to the free-field answer, with no counter-terms. Integrating over $\Sigma$ restricts the bilocal to configurations obeying the finite-$N$ constraints.

Both bilocals then map to AdS: the fluctuation $\eta$ of $G$ to the fields $\Phi_J$ as before, and $\Sigma$ to a second tower $\tilde\Phi_J$. Suitable normalizations make the coupling between the towers local, $\int\tilde\Phi_J\Phi_J$, with unit Jacobian, so the bulk theory is exact for any $N$, with $G_N=1/N$. Integrating out $\tilde\Phi_J$ order by order in $1/N$ gives back the earlier bulk action, but beyond perturbation theory these auxiliary fields seem necessary. The bulk is one fixed AdS background, with no sum over geometries or topologies, presumably a special feature of high-spin gravity. As a check, the amplitude of empty AdS, computed exactly on the lattice, vanishes for integer $N For the critical model in $2

Second, since $S^d$ is conformal to flat space, the map carries over to hyperbolic space, with $L_2$ normalizability as the bulk boundary condition. The sphere free energy then matches exactly and trivially: integrating out $\eta$, or in the bulk $\Phi_J$, forces its partner to vanish, so both sides give $Z=Z_\phi^N$, the partition function of $N$ free fields. It is a prefactor in front of the bulk path integral, with no classical or loop contribution. Earlier one-loop tests assumed canonical two-derivative kinetic terms for each spin; they matched for $U(N)$, but for $O(N)$ needed a shift of the bulk coupling. The bulk action here is quartic in derivatives, so the paper sees that match as a coincidence and suggests no shift.

To make the map rigorous, both sides must be regulated, the CFT by a cutoff on the Laplacian and the bulk by UV and IR cutoffs, each leaving finitely many modes and an $SO(d+1)$ symmetry. The regulators need not correspond: if each $SO(d+1)$ representation keeps equally many modes, the map splits into square blocks that are generically invertible. The paper argues that bulk cutoffs tied to the CFT's can match every count, giving a precise but impractical map.

Finally, at finite temperature the singlet projection requires integrating over a $U(N)$ holonomy, which the paper does not know how to map to the bulk in general. At large $N$ a saddle dominates: uniform eigenvalues in the low-temperature confined phase, reached by taking $N$ large before the volume, and eigenvalues near one in the deconfined phase. In the confined phase the bilocal behaves as if the thermal circle had length $N\beta$, so at large $N$ its expectation value is the zero-temperature propagator. The zero-temperature map then applies unchanged and gives bulk fields periodic in $\beta$: the low-temperature phase is high-spin gravity on thermal AdS.

The paper does not perform the integral over $\Sigma$, or $\tilde\Phi_J$, beyond perturbation theory, so the exact bulk theory keeps its auxiliary fields. Its regularization fixes mode counts rather than explicit regulators, and bulk boundary conditions for the high-spin fields remain subtle. The thermal map holds only at leading order in the large-$N$ saddle: at finite $N$ the holonomy fluctuates, and the deconfined phase, presumably a black hole, needs a different map, left to future work.

defs.html: A theory of $N$ scalar fields $\phi_I$ rotated as a vector by a $U(N)$ symmetry ($O(N)$ for real fields), studied in its singlet sector. The free model has no interactions; the critical model is the infrared fixed point reached from it by a quartic interaction $(\sum_I|\phi_I|^2)^2$, for $2<d<4$.

The part of the theory invariant under $U(N)$: operators built from $\sum_I\phi_I^*\phi_I$ and its derivatives, and the states they create. Only this sector has a gravity dual. On flat space or a sphere one simply restricts to it; at finite temperature imposing it requires integrating over a holonomy.

A gravitational theory with a massless field of every integer spin $J$, the graviton at $J=2$ among them, whose interactions are tied together by an infinite-dimensional gauge symmetry. Classically it is described by Vasiliev's equations. Here its coupling is $G_N=1/N$, and the paper's bulk theory is conjectured to be a gauge-fixed form of it.

Of an action: containing couplings between fields at separated points, not only products of fields and finitely many derivatives at one point. The bulk theory here has non-local interactions; a choice of field normalizations makes its quadratic part local.

A field of two spacetime points. Here $G(x_1,x_2)=\frac1N\sum_I\phi_I^*(x_1)\phi_I(x_2)$, the $U(N)$-invariant product of the scalars, its fluctuation $\eta=N(G-G_0)$ around the free propagator, and the multiplier $\Sigma(x_1,x_2)$. Every singlet operator is built from $G$, so it is the natural variable to map to the bulk.

Of a symmetric tensor field: divergence-free and with every trace zero. These conditions keep only the physical polarizations of a massless spin-$J$ field, so the bulk fields $\Phi_J$ are high-spin gauge fields in a fixed gauge.

Holding for every field configuration in the path integral, not only for solutions of the equations of motion. An off-shell map is a change of integration variables between field theory and bulk, so it relates the full path integrals, quantum effects included, and not only classical solutions.

A field introduced to impose a condition: integrating over it produces a delta function. Here the bilocal $\Sigma(x_1,x_2)$ imposes that $G$ equals the scalar bilinear. Keeping it as a field, rather than integrating it out, is what makes the bilocal theory exact at finite $N$.

The Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev model: $N$ Majorana fermions with random couplings among a few of them at a time, solvable at large $N$. Its standard treatment rewrites it, after averaging over the couplings, in terms of a bilocal $G(t_1,t_2)$ and a multiplier $\Sigma(t_1,t_2)$; the paper applies this “$G$–$\Sigma$” formalism to vector models.

Relations that the bilocal $G$ obeys only because it is built from $N$ vectors: as a matrix it has rank at most $N$, so the determinant of any $(N+1)\times(N+1)$ matrix $G(x_i,y_j)$ vanishes. They are invisible order by order in $1/N$, and the earlier large-$N$ bilocal integral ignores them.

A field with no dynamics of its own, whose path integral imposes a condition or produces an interaction. Here mostly the multiplier $\Sigma$ and its bulk image $\tilde\Phi_J$, which impose the finite-$N$ constraints; the critical model's Hubbard-Stratonovich field $\sigma$ is one too.

The paper's simplest regulator: space replaced by $V$ points, so that a bilocal is a $V\times V$ matrix and the continuum is $V\to\infty$. It cuts off both short and long distances. In the finite-temperature section the same letter $V$ denotes instead a spatial volume.

AdS with every high-spin fluctuation set to zero, $\Phi_J=0$, which corresponds to the bilocal sitting exactly at its large-$N$ value $G_0$. Its amplitude is the path-integral weight of that configuration; at finite $N$ it must vanish, because $G_0$ has rank larger than $N$.

The unitary representations of the Euclidean conformal group $SO(d+1,1)$ with complex dimension $\Delta=d/2+is$, $s$ real. Partial waves with these dimensions and every spin $J$ form a complete basis for normalizable functions of two points, which is what lets the bilocal be expanded and matched to bulk fields.

The shadow of an operator of dimension $\Delta$ has dimension $\tilde\Delta=d-\Delta$ and the same spin, and pairs with it in a conformally invariant way. The multiplier $\Sigma$ transforms like a product of two shadows of the free field, of dimension $(d+2)/2$, so its expansion is the shadow version of $\eta$'s.

Changes of variables in the bulk path integral that leave the physics unchanged. Here they are the normalizations $f_{\Delta,J}$ and $\tilde f_{\Delta,J}$ of each conformal component, not fixed by symmetry; the paper chooses them so that the bulk coupling of $\Phi_J$ to $\tilde\Phi_J$ is local, the Jacobian is one, and the quadratic action is local.

An auxiliary field $\sigma$ that turns a quartic interaction into a quadratic coupling: integrating over $\sigma$ in $\frac12\sigma\sum_I|\phi_I|^2-\frac N{4\lambda}\sigma^2$ gives back a quartic interaction of strength proportional to $\lambda/N$. The critical vector model is the limit $\lambda\to\infty$, reached at long distances.

$F=-\log Z$ for the theory on the round sphere $S^d$, one of the simplest observables of a CFT; in odd $d$ its finite part is universal and counts degrees of freedom. Here it is the regulated $Z_\phi^N$ of $N$ free fields, a normalization the paper fixes explicitly.

defs.html: $\mathbb{H}^{d+1}$, the space of constant negative curvature, which is Euclidean AdS. In coordinates $ds^2=dy^2+\sinh^2y\,d\Omega_d^2$ its conformal boundary at $y\to\infty$ is the sphere $S^d$, so it is the bulk for the CFT on $S^d$, as the upper half-space is for $\mathbb{R}^d$.

A stationary point of the action that dominates a path integral when the action is large, here proportional to $N$. At large $N$ the bilocal integral is dominated by the free propagator $G_0$, and the thermal holonomy integral by one distribution of eigenvalues.

The $U(N)$ matrix $U=\exp(i\int_0^\beta A_t\,dt)$ acquired by going once around the thermal circle in a background gauge field. Integrating over it projects the thermal trace onto singlets; its eigenvalue distribution tells the confined phase (uniform) from the deconfined one (all eigenvalues near one).

The low-temperature phase of the large-$N$ singlet theory, where only low-dimension singlets matter and the free energy does not grow with $N$; the holonomy's eigenvalues are spread uniformly. It is the phase reached by taking $N$ large before the volume, and the one the paper maps to thermal AdS.

The high-temperature phase, where the singlet constraint barely matters and the free energy is that of $N$ free fields, of order $N$; the holonomy is close to the identity. It is reached by taking the volume large before $N$, and presumably corresponds to a black hole in the bulk, which the paper leaves open.

Euclidean anti-de Sitter space with its Euclidean time made periodic, of period $\beta=1/T$, and no horizon. In AdS/CFT it is the bulk saddle of the low-temperature, confined phase, while a black hole describes the high-temperature one.

The propagator on a circle obtained from the one on a line by adding its translates by every multiple of the circumference, possibly with phases. Here the holonomy's phases cancel all images except those at multiples of $N\beta$, which disappear at large $N$.

The “clock” matrix is diagonal with entries $e^{2\pi iI/N}$; the “shift” matrix moves each basis vector cyclically to the next. Both are holonomies with uniformly spread eigenvalues, related by a gauge transformation. With the shift, the $N$ scalars on a circle of length $\beta$ become one scalar on a circle of length $N\beta$.

questions.a: $N$ is the number of complex scalars, and $G_N=1/N$ is the bulk coupling. In Sections 2 and 3, $V$ counts the points of the lattice regulator, so the continuum is $V\to\infty$; in Section 4 the same letter is a spatial volume. $d>2$ is the boundary dimension, the bulk is $AdS_{d+1}$, and the map takes different forms for $d>4$ and $d<4$. $\eta=N(G-G_0)$ is the bilocal's fluctuation, and $\Sigma$ the multiplier that fixes $G$.

questions.q: Why is the original map not valid at finite $N$?
questions.a: Because a bilocal built from $N$ vectors is a matrix of rank at most $N$, and the large-$N$ bilocal integral does not know this. Its weight $|\det G|^{N-V}$ converges only for $V\le N$, so the continuum limit exists only if $N$ is taken to infinity first. Order by order in $1/N$ the constraints are invisible; beyond perturbation theory they matter, for instance for the amplitude of empty AdS.

questions.q: Why does the finite-$N$ theory have no loop diagrams?
questions.a: The quadratic action pairs $\eta$ with $\Sigma$ and gives $\eta$ a propagator, but $\Sigma$ has none with itself. All vertices come from $W[\Sigma]$ and involve only $\Sigma$'s. A loop would need two $\Sigma$'s contracted together, so none exists: each connected correlator of $\eta$'s is a single tree diagram, which reproduces the free-field contractions directly. The same holds in the bulk for $\Phi_J$ and $\tilde\Phi_J$.

questions.q: What are the new bulk fields $\tilde\Phi_J$?
questions.a: They are the bulk image of the multiplier $\Sigma$: a second tower of transverse traceless spin-$J$ fields, coupled to the $\Phi_J$ through the local term $\int\tilde\Phi_J\Phi_J$ and interacting among themselves through $W$. They are auxiliary: integrated out order by order in $1/N$, they give back the earlier bulk action. Keeping them gives a consistent theory at finite $N$, because they impose the bulk version of the finite-$N$ constraints.

questions.q: What does the vanishing amplitude of empty AdS mean?
questions.a: Empty AdS, all $\Phi_J=0$, corresponds to $G=G_0$, the free propagator, which as a matrix on $V$ lattice points has rank $V$. A bilocal built from $N<V$ vectors cannot have that rank, so the measure must vanish there. The exact computation gives the naive large-$N$ factor times a product $\prod_k(k(N-k+1))^{V-k+1}$, which vanishes for integer $N<V$. In the continuum at finite $N$, empty AdS has zero amplitude.

questions.q: Does the finite-$N$ bulk theory need a sum over geometries or topologies?
questions.a: No. Even at finite $N$ the field theory maps to fields on one fixed AdS background, because the map is a change of variables in the path integral, and the finite-$N$ effects are carried by the auxiliary fields $\tilde\Phi_J$ instead. The paper suggests this is presumably a special feature of high-spin gravity theories; it does not discuss what replaces it in theories closer to Einstein gravity.

questions.q: Is the bulk theory Vasiliev's high-spin gravity?
questions.a: That is a conjecture, not shown here. With $\tilde\Phi_J$ integrated out perturbatively, the bulk action has the physical field content of Vasiliev's theory, and it was conjectured to be a gauge-fixed form of it on a fixed AdS background. Its kinetic terms are quartic in derivatives, so it carries extra off-shell modes, conjectured to be related to those of high-spin gravity. The paper uses no specific property of Vasiliev's equations.

questions.q: How does the critical vector model appear in the bulk?
questions.a: Through a boundary condition. The Hubbard-Stratonovich field $\sigma$ couples to $\eta(x,x)$, which the map relates to the leading boundary falloff of the scalar $\Phi_0$. At the infrared fixed point, $\lambda=\infty$, integrating over $\sigma$ sets that falloff to zero off-shell, so $\Phi_0$ starts at $z^{d/2}$, like the other spins, rather than at $z^{d-2}$. This mirrors how double-trace flows act in standard AdS/CFT.

questions.q: Where does the sphere free energy come from on the gravity side?
questions.a: From a prefactor. The fields $\Phi_J$ appear linearly, so integrating them out forces $\tilde\Phi_J=0$, and what remains is $e^{NW_\text{bulk}[0]}=Z_\phi^N$, the constant term of $W$ copied from the field theory. No classical action and no loop diagram contributes. Writing this constant in bulk language would need a bulk regularization, which the next subsection takes up.

questions.q: How does this compare with earlier one-loop tests of higher-spin holography?
questions.a: Without an action those tests could not compute the order-$N$ term, but they computed the one-loop term assuming canonical two-derivative kinetic terms for each spin. For $U(N)$ it vanished as expected; for $O(N)$ it equalled one real scalar's free energy, read as a shifted coupling $G_N\propto1/(N-1)$; other examples allowed no such shift. The bulk action here is quartic in derivatives, so the paper calls the $U(N)$ match a coincidence and suggests no shift.

questions.q: Why is it enough to match mode counts rather than the regulators themselves?
questions.a: Both regulated theories keep $SO(d+1)$, and the map respects it, so it splits into blocks, one for each $SO(d+1)$ representation. If both sides keep equally many modes in every representation, each block is square, and a generic square block is invertible. One can then restrict the CFT-to-AdS map to the surviving CFT modes, or the inverse map to the surviving bulk modes; both approach the continuum map as the cutoffs are removed.

questions.q: Why does the order of the large-$N$ and large-volume limits matter?
questions.a: The singlet theory has a transition at $T^{d-1}V\simeq N$, with $V$ here the spatial volume: below it the singlet bilocals dominate, with free energy of order $T^{2d-1}V^2$; above it the order $NV$ deconfined modes do. Taking $N$ large first keeps $T^{d-1}V\ll N$ at any temperature, the confined phase; taking the volume large first gives the deconfined phase. Only the former is mapped to the bulk.

questions.q: Why can't the same map describe the high-temperature phase?
questions.a: There the dominant holonomy is the identity, so each scalar is periodic and the bilocal is invariant under shifting either time argument by $\beta$ separately, not only both together. With the zero-temperature map it is unclear what this extra periodicity imposes on the bulk fields. The paper expects a different, black-hole-like geometry and a different map, as the non-vanishing traces of the holonomy also suggest, and leaves this open.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: It does not perform the integral over $\Sigma$ or $\tilde\Phi_J$ beyond perturbation theory, nor show that the bulk theory is Vasiliev's. Its regularization fixes mode counts, not explicit regulators suited to computation, and bulk boundary conditions for high-spin fields stay subtle. At finite temperature it maps only the confined phase, at leading order in the large-$N$ saddle; holonomy fluctuations at finite $N$, and the deconfined phase, are left open.
